events.title: The Hudson's Bay Company charter
events.note: Charles II grants the Hudson's Bay Company the lands draining into Hudson Bay, as Rupert's Land. France holds Canada and Acadia, and England and France both fish and claim Newfoundland. The charter is dated 2 May 1670 in the Old Style calendar England then used.

events.title: The Treaty of Utrecht
events.note: France gives up Hudson Bay, Newfoundland and "Nova Scotia or Acadia, with its ancient boundaries" to Great Britain, and keeps Cape Breton and the islands of the Gulf as Île Royale. The two powers never agree what Acadia's ancient boundaries were. Signed 31 March 1713 in the Old Style calendar; the exchange of ratifications was within four weeks but its day is not established.

events.title: The Treaty of Paris
events.note: France cedes Canada, Cape Breton and all the islands of the Gulf and River St. Lawrence to Great Britain. French rule in what is now Canada ends, except for fishing rights. Signed on 10 February; ratifications were exchanged on 10 March 1763.

events.title: The Royal Proclamation
events.note: Britain creates the Province of Quebec as a narrow band along the St. Lawrence and reserves the lands beyond the colonies for Indigenous nations. Newfoundland is given the Labrador coast, and Nova Scotia the islands of the Gulf.

events.title: St. John's Island
events.note: An order in council makes St. John's Island a colony separate from Nova Scotia. Its first governor, Walter Patterson, arrives in 1770.

events.title: The Quebec Act
events.note: Parliament enlarges Quebec to the Ohio, the Mississippi and the Hudson's Bay Company lands, and gives it back the Labrador coast. Its new civil government begins on 1 May 1775; the boundary took effect on assent.

events.title: The Treaty of Paris with the United States
events.note: Britain recognizes the United States, with a boundary through the Great Lakes and along the highlands south of the St. Lawrence. The treaty's vague lines leave disputes over New Brunswick and the country west of Lake Superior; nothing inside modern Canada changes hands. Signed 3 September 1783; in force 12 May 1784.

events.title: New Brunswick
events.note: Loyalists who fled the American Revolution press for their own colony, and an order in council divides Nova Scotia at the Missiguash River. Thomas Carleton's commission as governor follows on 16 August.

events.title: Cape Breton
events.note: Cape Breton is made a separate colony under Joseph DesBarres, who founds Sydney as its capital. The June order had made it a lieutenant-governorship subordinate to Nova Scotia.

events.title: Upper and Lower Canada
events.note: The Constitutional Act divides Quebec in two along the Ottawa River, giving the Loyalists of the west their own province. Upper Canada takes English law; Lower Canada keeps French civil law.

events.title: Prince Edward Island
events.note: The island's assembly renames St. John's Island after Prince Edward, and the King in Council confirms it. Its boundaries are unchanged.

events.title: The Labrador coast returns to Newfoundland
events.note: Parliament gives the Labrador coast and Anticosti back to Newfoundland to put the fishery under one government. Lower Canada keeps the Magdalen Islands.

events.title: The Convention of 1818
events.note: Britain and the United States draw their boundary along 49°N from Lake of the Woods to the Rocky Mountains, and leave the Oregon Country west of the mountains open to both. Signed 20 October 1818; in force 30 January 1819.

events.title: Cape Breton rejoins Nova Scotia
events.note: Cape Breton loses its separate government and is annexed to Nova Scotia again, over its residents' protests. Lieutenant-Governor Kempt proclaimed the change on 16 October 1820.

events.title: The fur trade merger
events.note: The Hudson's Bay Company and the North West Company merge after years of violent rivalry. Parliament gives the merged company an exclusive licence over the Indian Territories beyond Rupert's Land.

events.title: The Gulf shore returns to Lower Canada
events.note: Parliament moves the Gulf of St. Lawrence shore west of Anse-Sablon, and Anticosti, back to Lower Canada. Newfoundland keeps the coast east of the Anse-Sablon line and north of 52°N.

events.title: The Province of Canada
events.note: After the rebellions of 1837–38, Upper and Lower Canada are united as one province with one legislature. They remain Canada West and Canada East in practice.

events.title: The Webster–Ashburton Treaty
events.note: Britain and the United States settle the Maine–New Brunswick boundary and the line west of Lake Superior. The disputed claims arrive with the disputed layer; the ratifications were exchanged on 13 October 1842 by one treaty series and 15 October by another.

events.title: The Oregon Treaty
events.note: The boundary along 49°N is continued to the Pacific, leaving Vancouver Island wholly British. The joint occupation of the Oregon Country ends. Signed 15 June; in force 17 July 1846.

events.title: Vancouver Island
events.note: Britain grants Vancouver Island to the Hudson's Bay Company as a colony, to be settled against American expansion. Victoria becomes its capital.

events.title: British Columbia
events.note: The Fraser River gold rush brings thousands of miners, and Britain creates the mainland colony of British Columbia. The Act was passed on 2 August and proclaimed at Fort Langley on 19 November 1858.

events.title: The Stickeen Territories
events.note: Gold on the Stikine River prompts Britain to organize the land north of British Columbia as a territory under its governor. It lasts a year.

events.title: British Columbia extended
events.note: British Columbia takes in the Stickeen Territories south of 60°N and the Peace River country west of 120°W. The land north of 60°N returns to the Indian Territories.

events.title: Vancouver Island and British Columbia united
events.note: Debt and a slump after the gold rush force the two colonies into one, under the name British Columbia. New Westminster is the capital of the united colony at first.

events.title: Confederation
events.note: Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick unite as the Dominion of Canada. Everything north and west still belongs to Britain or to the Hudson's Bay Company.

events.title: Victoria becomes British Columbia's capital
events.note: The capital of the united colony moves from New Westminster to Victoria. No boundaries change.

events.title: Manitoba and the North-West Territories
events.note: Canada takes over Rupert's Land and the North-Western Territory from the Hudson's Bay Company. A small square around the Red River settlement becomes Manitoba.

events.title: British Columbia joins
events.note: British Columbia enters Confederation on the promise of a railway to the Pacific. Its boundaries are unchanged.

events.title: The San Juan award
events.note: Wilhelm I, arbitrating under the Treaty of Washington, finds for the American reading: the boundary runs through Haro Strait, and the San Juan Islands are American. The British garrison leaves in November 1872.

events.title: Prince Edward Island joins
events.note: Prince Edward Island joins Canada six years after Confederation. The island's boundaries are unchanged.

events.title: Ontario's provisional boundary
events.note: Ontario and the Dominion agree on a provisional line while Ontario's true limits are argued. Ontario extends north to 51°N and west to the meridian of Hunter's Island. The arrangement took effect when Ontario's order approved it on 9 July 1874; the memorandum itself is dated 26 June and the Dominion's approving order 8 July.

events.title: District of Keewatin
events.note: The Keewatin Act carves a district from the North-West Territories between Manitoba and Hudson Bay. The Lieutenant-Governor of Manitoba governs it from Winnipeg.

events.title: The Arctic islands
events.note: Britain transfers all its remaining North American possessions to Canada, except Newfoundland. The Arctic Archipelago joins the North-West Territories.

events.title: Manitoba enlarged
events.note: Manitoba grows west, north and east. Ontario claims the eastern part too, and the dispute goes to the Privy Council. The Act came into force on 1 July 1881 by proclamation of 13 June; a date of 23 December 1881 found in some secondary sources has no support in the Canada Gazette.

events.title: Provisional districts
events.note: Four districts are laid out on the prairies for settlers and the post office. Regina is chosen as the territorial capital.

events.title: Keewatin trimmed
events.note: A proclamation moves the land between Lake Winnipegosis and the Nelson River from Keewatin to the District of Saskatchewan. Keewatin now starts at Lake Winnipeg.

events.title: Ontario's boundary settled
events.note: Parliament confirms the Privy Council's ruling for Ontario. Its northern boundary becomes the English and Albany rivers, and the dispute with Manitoba ends.

events.title: Districts of the North
events.note: An order in council divides the northern territories into the districts of Ungava, Franklin, Mackenzie and Yukon. Athabaska grows east to 100°W.

events.title: Districts redrawn
events.note: A new order in council redraws the northern districts along the middle of the bays and straits. Keewatin takes Hudson Bay's western islands, and Franklin takes the Boothia and Melville peninsulas.

events.title: Yukon Territory and Quebec's first extension
events.note: The Klondike gold rush makes Yukon a separate territory with its capital at Dawson. Quebec extends north to the Eastmain River and east to Hamilton Inlet.

events.title: Yukon's boundary redrawn
events.note: Parliament moves Yukon's eastern boundary onto the mountain divides. It is the line Yukon still has.

events.title: The Sverdrup claim
events.note: The Fram returns from four winters in the archipelago. Otto Sverdrup had taken possession in the Norwegian king's name of the islands his expedition mapped west of Ellesmere, some 260,000 km² that Britain had transferred to Canada in 1880 without ever visiting. Norway pressed the claim from 1924.

events.title: The Alaska boundary award
events.note: An international tribunal settles the Alaska panhandle boundary, mostly in favour of the United States. The atlas draws the award line throughout, as NRCan does; the earlier claim lines arrive with the disputed layer. The Canadian claim itself is not drawn. The 1825 convention fixes no coordinate between 56°N and 141°W — it says "la crête des montagnes" and "les sinuosités de la côte" — and the tribunal answered by marking a map ("the line marked A B in red"), so the claim survives only on Map 37 of the British atlas filed on 23 September 1903. Tracing that map would put a ±5–10 km line into an atlas whose whole point is that its lines come from instruments. See docs/decisions.md.

events.title: Alberta and Saskatchewan
events.note: Two provinces are carved from the North-West Territories, each running from 49°N to 60°N. Keewatin is folded back into the territories, now run from Ottawa.

events.title: Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec extended
events.note: Three provinces extend north to Hudson Bay and Hudson Strait, taking most of Keewatin and the mainland of Ungava. Manitoba reaches 60°N.

events.title: Northwest Territories districts revised
events.note: An order of 1918 comes into force, leaving three districts: Mackenzie, Keewatin and Franklin. The District of Ungava disappears.

events.title: The Labrador boundary
events.note: The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council sets the boundary between Canada and Newfoundland in Labrador, and Newfoundland gets the whole Atlantic watershed. The report was delivered on 1 March 1927; His Majesty in Council approved it on 22 March 1927.

events.title: Norway recognises Canada's title
events.note: Norway recognises Canada's sovereignty over the Sverdrup Islands, closing the last foreign claim to the archipelago. Canada paid Sverdrup £6,700 for his charts and journals the same year.

events.title: Newfoundland joins
events.note: Newfoundland becomes Canada's tenth province after two referendums. Its boundaries, Labrador included, are those of 1927.

requires.because: Newfoundland joined from Commission of Government, under which Britain had governed it since 1934 (Newfoundland Act 1933, 24 & 25 Geo. V c. 2, UK); the Terms of Union were negotiated by delegations the Commission appointed and given effect by the British North America Act, 1949 (12, 13 & 14 Geo. VI c. 22, UK). A self-governing Newfoundland would have had to seek union through its own legislature.

events.title: Whitehorse becomes Yukon's capital
events.note: Yukon's capital moves from Dawson to Whitehorse, on the highway and the railway. No boundary changes.

events.title: The continental shelf agreement
events.note: Canada and Denmark divide the continental shelf between Ellesmere Island and Greenland, and stop the line at the water's edge on either side of Hans Island: points 122 and 123 leave a gap of about 1.4 km, because neither would concede the island. Both states then claimed it for half a century, by planting flags and, later, by leaving each other bottles of spirits.

events.title: The fishing zones and the grey zone
events.note: Canada and the United States each declare a 200-mile fishing zone, and publish boundaries in the Gulf of Maine that do not agree. The water between the two lines is fished under both flags and is known as the grey zone; Machias Seal Island, which Canada has lit since 1832, lies inside it. Canada's zone took effect on 1 January 1977 and the American one on 1 March 1977.

events.title: Nunavut
events.note: Nunavut is created from the eastern and northern Northwest Territories, following the Nunavut Land Claims Agreement. The old districts of Mackenzie, Keewatin and Franklin end.

events.title: Newfoundland and Labrador
events.note: A constitutional amendment renames the province Newfoundland and Labrador. Its boundaries are unchanged.

requires.because: The name was changed by the Constitution Amendment, 2001 (Newfoundland and Labrador), a Canadian amendment to the Terms of Union, which reaches only a province of Canada.

events.title: Yukon
events.note: The new Yukon Act drops "Territory" from the name. Its boundaries are unchanged.

events.title: Hans Island divided
events.note: Canada and the Kingdom of Denmark agree a land boundary across Hans Island, following a gully from north to south: the western part is Canadian and becomes part of Nunavut, the eastern part is Greenlandic. It is Canada's first new land boundary since 1949, and the last of the disputes in this atlas to close.

units.name: Acadia
units.note: Restored to France by the Treaty of Breda (1667) and handed over in 1670; its seat moved several times.
units.instrument: Treaty of Breda, 31 July 1667, art. X (restitution of Acadia to France).

units.name: Mainland Acadia (disputed)
units.note: Britain read Acadia's "ancient boundaries" to include this land; France held that it had ceded only the peninsula.
units.instrument: Treaty of Utrecht, art. XII ("with its ancient boundaries"); Historical Atlas of Canada timeline, 1713.

units.name: British Arctic Islands
units.instrument: British claims by discovery (Frobisher 1576–78, Davis, Hudson, Baffin), which NRCan's 1763 plate tints British; Rupert's Land and North-Western Territory Order (Imperial Order in Council, 23 June 1870, in force 15 July 1870), operative paragraph, which names no boundaries; Adjacent Territories Order (Imperial Order in Council, 31 July 1880), operative paragraph, transferring "all Islands adjacent" from 1 September 1880.
units.rationale: London and Ottawa treated the Arctic islands as outside the 1870 transfer, which is why Britain transferred them separately in 1880, so they are drawn apart from the North-Western Territory; the DCER editors note the 1821 and 1859 definitions could be read to include them, hence 0.7.

units.name: British Columbia
units.note: Proclaimed at Fort Langley; New Westminster was named the capital in 1859.
units.instrument: An Act to provide for the Government of British Columbia, 21 & 22 Vict. c. 99, s. I (2 August 1858): "bounded to the South by the Frontier of the United States of America, to the East by the main Chain of the Rocky Mountains, to the North by Simpson's River, and the Finlay Branch of the Peace River, and to the West by the Pacific Ocean, and shall include Queen Charlotte's Island"; proclaimed 19 November 1858.

units.name: British Columbia
units.instrument: An Act to define the Boundaries of the Colony of British Columbia, 26 & 27 Vict. c. 83, s. 3 (28 July 1863): bounded "to the North by the Sixtieth Parallel of North Latitude, and to the East, from the Boundary of the United States Northwards, by the Rocky Mountains and the One hundred and twentieth Meridian of West Longitude ... except Vancouver's Island and the Islands adjacent thereto."

units.name: British Columbia
units.note: Vancouver Island and the mainland colony united; the capital moved from New Westminster to Victoria in 1868.
units.instrument: British Columbia Act, 29 & 30 Vict. c. 67, ss. 3 and 8 (assented 6 August 1866), proclaimed 19 November 1866.

units.name: British Columbia
units.instrument: Proclamation of 25 May 1868 naming "the City of Victoria" the capital and seat of government of the united Colony of British Columbia.

units.name: Cape Breton
units.instrument: Commission to J.F.W. DesBarres as lieutenant-governor of Cape Breton, 9 August 1784 (Dictionary of Canadian Biography).

units.name: District of Franklin
units.instrument: Order in Council of 16 March 1918 (in force 1 January 1920), description of Keewatin: "thence southeasterly in a straight line to the most northerly point of cape Wolstenholme"; Franklin is the remainder of the Northwest Territories.
units.rationale: Nottingham Island lies at least 8 km north-east of the Frozen Strait–Cape Wolstenholme line, so it stays in Franklin; NRCan's maps from 1927 draw it in Keewatin.

units.name: District of Keewatin
units.note: Governed from Winnipeg by the Lieutenant-Governor of Manitoba and the Council of Keewatin.

units.name: District of Keewatin
units.note: A provisional district created by order, alongside the statutory District of Keewatin of 1876. Unlike the 1895 proposal, the 1897 order annexed a full description of the district, the Minister of Justice advised in 1898 that provisional districts needed no statute, and the 1918 order recites it as having defined "the provisional district of Keewatin". Statutory Keewatin rejoined the territories in 1905.
units.instrument: Order in Council P.C. 1897-3388 (18 December 1897, Canada Gazette 14 May 1898, pp. 2613–2614), annexed description "KEEWATIN"; cancelled from 1 January 1920 by the order of 16 March 1918.

units.name: District of Keewatin
units.note: Re-annexed to the North-West Territories, which were governed from Ottawa.

units.name: District of Ungava
units.instrument: Order in Council P.C. 1897-3388 (18 December 1897), description "UNGAVA" (bounded by the middle of Hudson Strait and Keewatin's mid-water line); Quebec Boundaries Extension Act, 1912, 2 Geo. V c. 45, s. 2 (the new boundary runs "along the shores"); Order in Council of 16 March 1918, cancelling the 1897 order and in force 1 January 1920.
units.rationale: The 1912 Act moved only the mainland to Quebec and the 1897 order defining Ungava stood until 1 January 1920, so the islands remain a district until then; NRCan already splits them between Keewatin and Franklin, and the Act excludes islands only by following the shore, hence 0.8.

units.name: Hans Island (Canada's claim)
units.instrument: Agreement between Canada and Denmark relating to the delimitation of the continental shelf, 17 December 1973, whose line runs to point 122 (-66.4833, 80.82) and resumes at point 123 (-66.4383, 80.83).
units.rationale: The agreement's gap is the dispute: both states claimed the whole island, and the 1:1M source draws it as wholly Canadian.

units.name: Hans Island / Tartupaluk (Denmark's claim)
units.instrument: The same agreement of 17 December 1973, read the other way: Denmark claimed the island as part of Greenland, whose Inughuit have hunted from it as Tartupaluk.
units.rationale: Denmark's claim covered the same whole island, which is why the shelf line had to stop at its shore.

units.name: Île Royale
units.note: Cape Breton, with Île Saint-Jean (Prince Edward Island) as a dependency from 1720.
units.instrument: Treaty of Utrecht, art. XIII: "the island called Cape Breton, as also all others, both in the mouth of the river of St. Lawrence, and in the gulph of the same name, shall hereafter belong of right to the French".

units.name: Cape Breton and St. John's Island
units.instrument: Treaty of Paris, 10 February 1763, art. IV.

units.name: Labrador interior (Canada, for Quebec)
units.note: Drawn as the country behind a one-statute-mile shore strip. The strip is a hairline at this scale, so what the map shows is the claim's effect: the interior Canada said was Quebec's.
units.instrument: Canada's case before the Judicial Committee, 1927: the boundary should be "a line to be drawn from the eastern headland of the bay or harbour of Blanc Sablon on the south to Cape Chidley on the north at a distance from high-water mark on the seacoast of the Peninsula of Labrador of one mile".
units.rationale: Canada read the 1763 grant as a grant for administering a migratory fishery, so "the coast" meant the strip of shore that fishery used, and everything behind it stayed Quebec's.

units.name: Labrador (Newfoundland's claim)
units.instrument: Newfoundland's case before the Judicial Committee, 1927: "a line drawn due north from Ance Sablon as far as the fifty-second degree of north latitude, and … traced from thence northwards to Cape Chidley along the crest of the watershed of the rivers flowing into the Atlantic Ocean".
units.rationale: Newfoundland argued that occupation of a sea-coast carries the country draining into it, which is the reading the Judicial Committee adopted in 1927.

units.name: Lower Canada
units.instrument: Constitutional Act, 31 Geo. III c. 31, and Order in Council of 24 August 1791, in force 26 December 1791.

units.name: Lower Canada
units.instrument: 6 Geo. IV c. 59, s. IX (22 June 1825): the coast "to the westward of a line to be drawn due north and south from the bay or harbour of Ance Sablon inclusive, as far as the fifty-second degree of north latitude, with the Island of Anticosti" re-annexed to Lower Canada.

units.name: Machias Seal Island and the grey zone
units.note: The 1984 International Court of Justice judgment divided the Gulf of Maine seaward of here and left the island and this water untouched. The two lines cross near the northern end, so a small area is claimed by neither state rather than by both.
units.instrument: Canada's Fishing Zones of Canada (Zone 5) Order, C.R.C. c. 1548, Sch. I, Area 2 (42 points), and the United States' line published at 60 Fed. Reg. 43825 (12 points). The two lines share their end points.
units.rationale: Both states publish a line, the lines differ, and neither has moved: the ground between them is the dispute, and it is the only one in this atlas that is still open.

units.name: Manitoba
units.instrument: Manitoba Act, 1870, 33 Vict. c. 3, s. 1 (assented 12 May 1870, in force 15 July 1870).
units.rationale: Section 1 fixes the province on the 96° and 99° meridians and the 49° and 50°30' parallels, so the box is drawn on those lines; NRCan's box is drafted 2–3 km off them.

units.name: Manitoba's eastern claim
units.note: The eastern limit is given here as the 89°09'W meridian that the Dominion pressed. The instruments name a river confluence rather than a longitude, so the meridian is a reading, not a quotation.
units.instrument: An Act to provide for the extension of the boundaries of the Province of Manitoba, 44 Vict. c. 14, s. 4 (in force 1 July 1881), carrying Manitoba east to "the westerly boundary of the Province of Ontario".
units.rationale: The Act sent Manitoba east to a boundary Ontario's own arbitration had already fixed elsewhere, so each province read the same words as reaching the other's line.

units.name: New Brunswick
units.note: Saint John served as capital until the government moved to Fredericton in 1788.
units.instrument: Order of His Majesty in Council, 18 June 1784: the land north of the Missiguash "erected into a Government under the Name of New Brunswick"; commission to Thomas Carleton, 16 August 1784.

units.name: New Brunswick
units.instrument: British North America Act, 1867, 30 & 31 Vict. c. 3, ss. 5 and 7.

units.name: Canada (New France)
units.note: The colony of Canada, claiming the St. Lawrence and Great Lakes basins (the pays d'en haut) and Labrador's Atlantic slope.
units.instrument: French royal government of New France from 1663 (Édit de création du Conseil souverain, April 1663); no instrument fixed its limits.

units.name: Canada
units.note: Under British military government since the capitulation of Montreal (8 September 1760).
units.instrument: Treaty of Paris, 10 February 1763, art. IV: "his Most Christian Majesty cedes and guaranties to his said Britannick Majesty, in full right, Canada, with all its dependencies, as well as the island of Cape Breton, and all the other islands and coasts in the gulph and river of St. Lawrence".

units.name: Newfoundland
units.note: English fishing settlements on the east coast and the French colony of Plaisance, founded 1662. NRCan's 1667 plate stripes the whole island.
units.instrument: No instrument settled it: England's claim rested on Cabot (1497) and Gilbert (1583), France's on its colony at Plaisance (1662).

units.name: Newfoundland
units.note: British, with French fishing rights on the French Shore; governed by naval commodores, with no formal colonial government until 1825. St. John's was the seat in practice.
units.instrument: Treaty of Utrecht, art. XIII: "The island called Newfoundland, with the adjacent islands, shall from this time forward, belong of right wholly to Britain".

units.name: Newfoundland
units.instrument: Royal Proclamation, 7 October 1763: "all that Coast, from the River St. John's to Hudson's Streights, together with the Islands of Anticosti and Madelaine, and all other smaller Islands lying upon the said Coast, under the care and Inspection of our Governor of Newfoundland."

units.name: Newfoundland
units.instrument: Quebec Act, 14 Geo. III c. 83, s. I (the Labrador coast, Anticosti and the Magdalens annexed to Quebec).

units.name: Newfoundland
units.instrument: 49 Geo. III c. 27, s. XIV (30 March 1809): the coast of Labrador "from the river St. John to Hudson's Streights, and the said Island of Anticosti" re-annexed to Newfoundland, "except the islands of Madelaine".

units.name: Newfoundland
units.note: A self-governing British colony, a Dominion from 1907, and under a Commission of Government from 1934. How far its Labrador coast ran inland was not defined until 1927; the strip shown follows NRCan's maps.

units.name: Newfoundland
units.note: A Dominion under a Commission of Government from 1934. The Privy Council's line of 1927 has never been demarcated, and Quebec has not formally accepted it.

units.name: Lands outside European claims
units.note: The Pacific slope, the Arctic and Missouri drainage, and the Arctic islands, held by Indigenous nations.

units.name: Indian Reserve
units.note: Reserved for Indigenous nations under the Crown's protection; settlement and private purchase forbidden.
units.instrument: Royal Proclamation, 7 October 1763: "all the Lands and Territories not included within the Limits of Our said Three new Governments, or within the Limits of the Territory granted to the Hudson's Bay Company, as also all the Lands and Territories lying to the Westward of the Sources of the Rivers which fall into the Sea from the West and North West".

units.name: Indian Territories
units.note: Under the Hudson's Bay Company's exclusive trading licence; named the North-Western Territory by the 1859 Indian Territories Act.
units.instrument: An Act for regulating the Fur Trade, 1 & 2 Geo. IV c. 66 (2 July 1821), s. VI (jurisdiction "within the said Indian Territories"); licence of exclusive trade, 5 December 1821.

units.name: North-Western Territory
units.note: Never defined in law; British territory under the Hudson's Bay Company's trade.
units.instrument: Indian Territories Act, 1859, 22 & 23 Vict. c. 26 (the name); no instrument defined its limits.

units.name: North-West Territories
units.note: Governed from Manitoba by its Lieutenant-Governor.

units.name: North-West Territories
units.note: The seat moved from Fort Livingstone to Battleford in 1877–78.

units.name: North-West Territories
units.note: Regina was named the seat in 1882 and took over from Battleford on 27 March 1883.

units.name: North-West Territories
units.instrument: Order in Council P.C. 1895-2640 (2 October 1895, Canada Gazette 19 October 1895, p. 684), Keewatin paragraph: the Minister "recommends that at the next Session of Parliament a Bill be introduced" to add about 470,000 square miles to Keewatin; the Ungava paragraph includes only islands "within a distance of three sea miles from the coast". Keewatin's limits were fixed by the Keewatin Act, 39 Vict. c. 21, s. 1 (R.S.C. 1886, c. 53).
units.rationale: The 1895 order drew the four new districts directly but only proposed a bill to enlarge statutory Keewatin, and no bill was introduced (recited in P.C. 1897-3388), so this land stays outside any district until the 1897 order; NRCan draws the enlargement as if it had taken effect.

units.name: Nova Scotia
units.note: Captured in 1710 and ceded in 1713; Halifax replaced Annapolis Royal as capital in 1749.
units.instrument: Treaty of Utrecht, 11 April 1713 (31 March Old Style), art. XII: "all Nova Scotia or Acadia, with its ancient boundaries, as also the city of Port Royal, now called Annapolis Royal".

units.name: Nova Scotia
units.note: The dispute over mainland Acadia ends with the French cession.
units.instrument: Treaty of Paris, 10 February 1763, art. IV.

units.name: Nova Scotia
units.instrument: Royal Proclamation, 7 October 1763: "to annex the Islands of St. John's and Cape Breton, or Isle Royale, with the lesser Islands adjacent thereto, to our Government of Nova Scotia."

units.name: Nova Scotia
units.instrument: Commission to the Earl of Dalhousie, 27 April 1820, and Lieutenant-Governor Sir James Kempt's proclamation of 16 October 1820 ending Cape Breton's separate government.

units.name: Nova Scotia
units.instrument: British North America Act, 1867, 30 & 31 Vict. c. 3, ss. 5 and 7.

units.name: Nunavut
units.note: The 1:1M source draws the whole island in Canada, so the Greenlandic part is cut from Nunavut for the map to agree with the treaty. That part is about 0.57 km², below the 2 km² minimum the display copy keeps, so the drawn polygon does not change: the change is in the row, not the picture. The island's outline at 1:1M is generalized, so the treaty's roughly even division comes out closer to a third–two thirds. The boundary is drawn, not surveyed.
units.instrument: Agreement between Canada and the Kingdom of Denmark together with Greenland, 14 June 2022, art. 4(3): the land boundary follows the points listed in Annex 3, leaving the eastern part to Greenland.

units.name: Ontario
units.instrument: British North America Act, 1867, 30 & 31 Vict. c. 3, ss. 5 and 6 (Upper Canada becomes Ontario).

units.name: Ontario's northern claim
units.instrument: Award of the arbitrators, 3 August 1878 (Sir Francis Hincks, Sir Edward Thornton and Chief Justice Harrison), carried into law by 52 & 53 Vict. c. 28 (1889) after the Judicial Committee's report of 11 August 1884.
units.rationale: Ontario claimed north to the Albany River and west to the North-West Angle meridian, which is what the arbitrators awarded and what Parliament eventually confirmed.

units.name: Ontario–Manitoba disputed area
units.note: Claimed by Manitoba under the 1881 Act and by Ontario under the 1878 arbitration. The Privy Council found for Ontario in 1884; Parliament confirmed it in 1889.

units.name: Columbia District (British claim)
units.note: The Columbia's course below 49°N is map-read to about ±3 km: Canada1Water carries no American reaches, so the river cannot be taken from the same source as the rest of the atlas.
units.instrument: Britain's standing offer of 1818, 1824, 1826 and 1844: the boundary to follow 49°N to the Columbia and then the river to the sea, leaving the country north of it British.
units.rationale: Britain never claimed south of the Columbia as of right; the Hudson's Bay Company held the district under the licences of 1821 and 1838, and the river was the line it offered four times.

units.name: Oregon Country (United States' claim)
units.instrument: Convention of London, 20 October 1818, art. III (country "Westward of the Stony Mountains" free and open to both, without prejudice to any claim); the American claim ran to 54°40'N, the southern limit of the Russian claim under the conventions of 1824 and 1825.
units.rationale: The United States claimed the whole country between the Spanish line of 42°N (Adams–Onís, 1819) and the Russian line of 54°40'N, which is the frame contemporaries argued inside.

units.name: St. John's Island
units.instrument: Order of His Majesty in Council, 28 June 1769, approving a separate government for the island of St. John.

units.name: Province of Canada
units.note: The seat moved: Kingston 1841, Montreal 1844, Toronto 1849, Quebec 1851, Toronto 1855, Quebec 1859, Ottawa 1865.
units.instrument: Act of Union, 3 & 4 Vict. c. 35, s. I (assented 23 July 1840), proclaimed by Lord Sydenham on 10 February 1841.

units.name: Province of Quebec
units.instrument: Royal Proclamation, 7 October 1763: "bounded on the Labrador Coast by the River St. John, and from thence by a Line drawn from the Head of that River through the Lake St. John, to the South end of the Lake Nipissim; from whence the said Line, crossing the River St. Lawrence, and the Lake Champlain, in 45. Degrees of North Latitude, passes along the High Lands ... and also along the North Coast of the Baye des Chaleurs, and the Coast of the Gulph of St. Lawrence to Cape Rosieres, and from thence crossing the Mouth of the River St. Lawrence by the West End of the Island of Anticosti, terminates at the aforesaid River of St. John."

units.name: Province of Quebec
units.instrument: Quebec Act, 14 Geo. III c. 83, s. I (assented 22 June 1774): Quebec extends "Northward to the Southern Boundary of the Territory granted to the Merchants Adventurers of England, trading to Hudson's Bay; and also all such Territories, Islands, and Countries, which have, since the tenth of February, one thousand seven hundred and sixty-three, been made Part of the Government of Newfoundland".

units.name: Quebec
units.instrument: British North America Act, 1867, 30 & 31 Vict. c. 3, ss. 5 and 6 (Lower Canada becomes Quebec).

units.name: Rupert's Land
units.note: Granted to the Hudson's Bay Company by royal charter; France contested the bay posts until 1713.
units.instrument: Royal Charter of the Hudson's Bay Company, 2 May 1670 (Old Style): "all the Landes Countryes and Territoryes upon the Coastes and Confynes of the Seas ... that lye within the entrance of the Streightes commonly called Hudsons Streightes".

units.name: Rupert's Land
units.note: Granted to the Hudson's Bay Company by royal charter in 1670.

units.name: San Juan Islands (disputed)
units.note: One polygon for both claims: the ground at stake is the same islands whichever channel is meant. The German Emperor awarded them to the United States on 21 October 1872.
units.instrument: Oregon Treaty, 15 June 1846, art. I: the line runs "to the middle of the channel which separates the continent from Vancouver's Island; and thence southerly through the middle of the said channel, and of Fuca's Straits to the Pacific Ocean".
units.rationale: Britain read the channel as Rosario Strait and the United States as Haro Strait; the islands between them were claimed by both and occupied by both from 1859.

units.name: Stickeen Territories
units.instrument: Imperial Order in Council, 19 July 1862: "bounded to the West and South West by the Frontier of Russian America, to the south and South East by the boundary of British Columbia, to the East by the 125th meridian of West Longitude, and to the north by the 62nd parallel of North latitude".

units.name: The Sverdrup Islands (Norwegian claim)
units.note: Norway never claimed the islands as a state: its 1930 note says "it is not the intention of his Government to claim sovereignty". The row is drawn as the claim the expedition made and Norway pressed on its behalf.
units.instrument: Acts of possession by Otto Sverdrup's second Fram expedition, 1898–1902, pressed by Norway in the notes of 29 October 1924 and 12 March 1925.
units.rationale: The islands were mapped and claimed by the expedition, and Norway never abandoned the claim until 1930; Canada's own title rested on the 1880 transfer of islands no one had surveyed.

units.name: Upper Canada
units.note: Newark (Niagara-on-the-Lake) was the capital until 1796; York is now Toronto.
units.instrument: Constitutional Act, 31 Geo. III c. 31, and Order in Council of 24 August 1791 (the dividing line), in force 26 December 1791 by proclamation of 18 November 1791.

units.name: Vancouver Island
units.instrument: Royal Grant of Vancouver's Island to the Hudson's Bay Company, letters patent of 13 January 1849.
